messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a **high‑level recipe** – written as if I were writing a small script – that shows exactly how you’d chain together the two “tools” you described so that a real person (or bot) ends up placing a *burger + fries* order at Mc D’s.

---

### 1️⃣ Find the right API

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `search_api_calls(query)` | Queries the web / developer portals & returns URLs/endpoints that look useful |
| `execute_call(call_string)` | Takes a fully‑formed REST/GraphQL query (as plain text) and runs it |

#### Step 1a – Search

```text
query = "McDonald's online ordering API"
results = search_api_calls(query)
```

Typical output might contain links such as:
- <https://developers.mcdonalds.com/api>
- <https://api.doordash.com/v2/orders>   *(DoorDash partner API)*
- <https://www.udemy.com/course/mc-dons-api/> *(example docs)*

Pick the most reliable public entry point.  
If there isn’t a public Mc D’s API, fall back on a delivery platform that partners with them (e.g., DoorDash, Uber Eats).

#### Step 1b – Inspect the documentation

Open the chosen link manually (or let your own scraper read the HTML) and locate:

| Piece | Why it matters |
|-------|----------------|
| Base URL (`https://api.example.com`) | Needed for all subsequent calls |
| Auth flow (OAuth2? API Key?) | You’ll need a bearer/token |
| Endpoints for: `<GET>/menu`, `<POST>/cart/add`, `<POST>/checkout` | Core actions |
| Payload schema | JSON structure required for each call |

Store this information in variables for later reuse.

---

### 2️⃣ Authenticate

Assume the service uses OAuth2 Client Credentials grant.

```text
call_str = """
POST https://api.example.com/oauth/token
Headers: {
  "Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded",
  "Accept": "application/json"
}
Body: {
  "grant_type": "client_credentials",
  "client_id": "<YOUR_CLIENT_ID>",
  "client_secret": "<YOUR_SECRET>"
}
"""
response = execute_call(call_str)
access_token = response.json()["access_token"]
```

Keep `access_token` handy—prepend it to every future request via the `Authorization: Bearer …` header.

---

### 3️⃣ Build the Order

#### 3a – Get menu IDs

```text
call_str = f"""
GET https://api.example.com/menu
Headers: {{
  "Authorization": "Bearer {access_token}",
  "Accept": "application/json"
}}
"""
resp = execute_call(call_str)
menu_items = resp.json()          # List/dict of items
burger_item = next(i for i in menu_items if i["name"] == "Big Mac")
fries_item  = next(i for i in menu_items if i["name"] == "Fries")
```

(Replace `"Big Mac"` with whatever burger you want.)

#### 3b – Add items to cart

```text
add_burger = f"""
POST https://api.example.com/cart/items
Headers: {{
  "Authorization": "Bearer {access_token}",
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
  "Accept": "application/json"
}}
Body: {{
  "itemId": "{burger_item['id']}",
  "quantity": 1,
  "options": []            /* e.g., extra cheese */
}}
"""

add_fries = f"""
POST https://api.example.com/cart/items
Headers: {{ ... same headers ... }}
Body: {{
  "itemId": "{fries_item['id']}",
  "quantity": 1,
  "size": "Large"
}}
"""

execute_call(add_burger)
execute_call(add_fries)
```

After both calls, the cart contains the desired combo.

---

### 4️⃣ Checkout

Most platforms require shipping address, phone, and payment method. For illustration assume a saved card id exists.

```text
order_payload = {
  "deliveryAddress": {
      "street": "123 Main St",
      "city": "Anytown",
      "state": "CA",
      "zipCode": "90210"
  },
  "phoneNumber": "+15551234567",
  "paymentMethodId": "card_abc123",        # previously stored
  "notes": "Please ring bell."
}

call_str = f"""
POST https://api.example.com/order/create
Headers: {{
  "Authorization": "Bearer {access_token}",
  "Content-Type": "application/json",
  "Accept": "application/json"
}}
Body: {json.dumps(order_payload)}
"""
order_resp = execute_call(call_str)
print("Order placed! Tracking #: ", order_resp.json().get("tracking_number"))
```

That single payload tells the system what to deliver, where, and how to pay.

---

### 5️⃣ Optional: Poll for status

Some APIs expose `/orders/{id}/status`. Loop until `delivered`.

```text
while True:
    status_call = f"""
    GET https://api.example.com/order/status?id={order_resp.id}
    Headers: {{
       "Authorization": "Bearer {access_token}"
    }}
    """
    status_res = execute_call(status_call)
    state = status_res.json()['state']
    print(f"Status: {state}")
    if state.lower() == "delivered":
         break
    sleep(30)           # poll every half minute
```

---

## Recap of the Flow

| Phase | Action | Tool Used |
|-------|--------|-----------|
| Discover | Search for suitable APIs | `search_api_calls()` |
| Pick & Read Docs | Choose best candidate & understand auth & routes | Manual inspection / scraping |
| Authorize | Obtain bearer token | `execute_call()` |
| Browse Menu | Pull item catalog | `execute_call()` |
| Cart Ops | Add burger+fries | `execute_call()` |
| Finalise | Submit order | `execute_call()` |
| Track | Poll status | `execute_call()` |

With just those two primitives you can programmatically place almost any kind of order—provided the target vendor exposes a machine‑readable interface. In practice you’ll also need to handle errors, rate limits, retries, and secure storage of credentials/payments—but the skeleton above demonstrates the core logic.
